tagline: One Agent tool, two behaviors: **omit subagent_type** and you get a fork of yourself; **set it** and you get an isolated specialist.
summary: When Claude Code calls its **Agent tool**, a single parameter decides everything. With **subagent_type set**, it spawns a **subagent**: a separate agent with its own system prompt, its own tool list, and a **fresh, empty context**. With subagent_type **omitted**, it spawns a **fork**: a background copy of the calling agent that **inherits the entire conversation so far**. Same tool, opposite starting points.

sections.heading: The parameter that changes everything
body: A **subagent** starts from its **agent definition** — a system prompt and tool list written for one job (a code reviewer, a test runner, an explorer). It knows **only what's in the prompt you pass it**. The conversation that led up to spawning it does not exist for it.

A **fork** starts from **everything**. It is the same agent, with the same conversation history, continuing in the background. You don't have to explain anything to it — it was, in every sense, **there for the whole conversation**.

sections.heading: Why fork instead of just doing the work?
body: Two reasons: **parallelism** and **context protection**. A fork runs in the **background**, so the parent can keep working — or spawn several forks at once for independent subtasks.

And a fork's tool calls — file reads, searches, build output — **stay in the fork's context**. The parent receives only the fork's **final message**. Heavy exploration that would flood the parent's context window happens out-of-line, and only the conclusion comes back.

sections.heading: Continuing a spawned agent
body: Both forks and subagents can be **continued** after they finish: messaging a completed agent by name or ID resumes it **with its context intact**. A **new** Agent call with a subagent_type, by contrast, always **starts fresh** — nothing carries over from the previous spawn.

diagram.caption: The **subagent_type** parameter is the entire difference: omitted → fork (inherits everything); set → subagent (fresh start).

nodes.label: Parent conversation
nodes.note: The main conversation — user messages, assistant turns, tool results. This is what a fork inherits and a subagent never sees.

nodes.label: Agent tool call
nodes.note: The parent decides to delegate: it calls the **Agent tool** with a prompt describing the work.

nodes.label: subagent_type set?
nodes.note: **The fork-in-the-road.** This one parameter decides whether the child starts with **everything** or **nothing**.

nodes.label: Fork — inherits full context
nodes.note: A **copy of the parent**, conversation and all, running in the background. No prompt-writing needed to bring it up to speed — it already knows.

nodes.label: Subagent — fresh context
nodes.note: A **different agent**: its own system prompt (from the agent definition), its own tool restrictions, and an **empty context** except for the prompt it was passed.

nodes.label: Final message returns
nodes.note: Either way, only the child's **final message** comes back as the tool result. Its tool calls, file reads, and intermediate work stay in **its** context.

scenarios.title: Delegate background work to a **fork of yourself**
scenarios.note: The fork **already knows the whole conversation** — the prompt only needs to say what to do next, not re-explain the context. Its exploration stays out of the parent's context window.

scenarios.title: Delegate a bounded task to a **specialist subagent**
scenarios.note: The subagent knows **only its agent definition and the prompt**. Everything it needs must be in that prompt — file paths, requirements, constraints. That's the cost of isolation, and also the point of it.

misconceptions.myth: The Agent tool always creates a fresh, isolated agent.
misconceptions.reality: Only when **subagent_type is set**. Omit it and the spawned agent is a **fork** — it inherits the **full conversation context** of its parent.
misconceptions.why: The tool is one tool with two modes, and the mode switch is a parameter you can simply not notice. This exact confusion motivated this site.

misconceptions.myth: A fork shares live state with the parent — what the parent learns next, the fork knows too.
misconceptions.reality: A fork inherits the conversation **as of the moment it was spawned**. After that, parent and fork **diverge** — new parent context does not flow into the running fork.
misconceptions.why: 'Inherits full context' is easy to read as 'shares context'. It's a copy at spawn time, not a live link.

misconceptions.myth: The parent (and the user) can watch everything a fork or subagent does.
misconceptions.reality: Children run in the **background**. The parent receives the **final message only**, as a tool result — and that message isn't even shown to the user unless the parent relays it.
misconceptions.why: The work is real and the tools really run; it's the **visibility** that's scoped. What crosses the boundary is deliberately minimal.
